newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK property developers "too greedy" for aesthetics.
newsitem.headline: HK property developers "too greedy" for aesthetics.

text.p: A senior American architect accused Hong Kong residential property developers on Wednesday of being too greedy to invest in aesthetic touches, so that rashes of ugly flats defaced the fast-growing Asian city.
Developers in crowded Hong Kong were spurred by rocketing returns on investment, Raj Barr-Kumar, president of the American Institute of Architects (AIA), said.
"(These) residential estates are ugly. Any large residential estate is dehumanising and the more repetition (of blocks of flats) there is, the more it is so and that is objectionable."

The AIA has 60,000 individual members, with nearly 100 based in Hong Kong. Barr-Kumar denounced a lack of landscaping and greening in many of Hong Kong's sprawling residential complexes, calling it an effect of raw capitalism.

"Demand on housing is very intense...and the developer would have to charge the buyer more (for improvements)," Barr-Kumar said in an interview with Reuters during a visit to the British colony where he met the Hong Kong Institute of Architects.
"I don't see much change in that. In a demand-driven market there is no time to stop and ask for amenities," he said.
In Hong Kong, a full return on building investment takes only seven years, compared to 30 years in other countries like the United States.
The rate of return on an investment is roughly 50 percent, a phenomenally high amount, he said.
Barr-Kumar also said that Hong Kong's provision of facilities for handicapped people was far behind standards in the United States.
"How could someone in a wheelchair hobble their way up the stairs to take the Star Ferry?" he said referring to the terminal for services between Hong Kong island and Kowloon.
The AIA and the Architectural Society of China are jointly developing common standards for the Union of International Architects, a non-governmental agency under the United Nations.
Barr-Kumar was on his way to China, where there was an urgent need to understand modern technology, he said.
